item.title: IDEA: The Gifts Chefs and Bartender Actually Want This Year
item.description:
Source: Eater
This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry, in an issue presented by Square. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. The Gifts Chefs and Bartender Actually Want This Year Streetwear cooking shoes, a perfect pepper mill, and more If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. This is not your average “gifts for foodies” round-up. We know that you’ve probably been given a few too many wine glasses and cookbooks. “As a professional, I don’t want to be gifted introductory-level items that will ultimately go unused,” says Storm Brunni, private dining director at Barolo Grill in Denver. That’s why, for our guide, we’ve consulted you, the hospitality pros, about what you actually would like to receive this year. New shoes for service. “I’m getting all of my favorite people the new high-top kitchen shoes by Chuck Taylor in leather anti-slip. They’re cool enough to complete your streetwear look, functional enough to wear in the dining room, kitchen, or work, and comfy enough to wear as a commuter.” —Jonathon Sawyer, chef at Kindling in Chicago An industry-favorite hand cream. “Between constant handwashing, citrus, chiles, and hot pans, hospitality hands take a beating. Add a heated neck massager to use on the couch after a midnight close, and you’ve basically given someone a spa day.” —Antelmo Ambrosio, executive chef at Casa Oaxaca in New York City Something for the coffee nerds. “It’s definitely a splurge, but I buy myself the Onyx Coffee Advent Calendar every year. A lot of hospitality pros nerd out about coffee, and Onyx is one of the best roasters. They fill the calendar with individual portions of beans (enough for two people) with different origins, roasts, and processes every day. Everything is roasted on a schedule so that when you’re brewing each one, the coffee is at its peak that day. The calendar has some of their signature coffees, alongside one-offs that you’ll never be able to get again, and I’ve tried some of the best coffees of my life in past calendars.” —Katie Renshaw, owner of Bar Bambi in Chicago An upgrade for kitchen organization. “I love this automatic tape dispenser. Gift it with a nice fresh box of Sharpies.” —Kevin Beary, beverage director of Gus’ Sip & Dip, Kitty’s Cosmopolitan Club, Three Dots and a Dash in Chicago The gift of longer-lasting produce. “Vejibag is a family-owned business, run by a small team of women who create 100 percent organic cotton bags designed to keep produce fresher for longer at home. They genuinely work and are an amazing addition to any kitchen.” —Lauren DeSteno, executive chef at Ai Fiori in New York City A tool for operators who know there’s always something that needs fixing. “I was given a precision screwdriver from HOTO Tools and now I’m obsessed with the brand and their design aesthetic. So many things in the restaurants need little fixes all the time and the 3.6V Electric Screwdriver Kit Pro has all the bits you could need. I also love their rotary drill for polishing plateware with chips/scratches for work.” —Zach Engel, chef at Galit and Cafe Yaya in Chicago Gifts with a personal touch. “As a general manager some of the top staff requests I’ve received are for nice wine keys (it’s an even nicer touch if they’re engraved) and custom server books.” —John Schneekloth, general manager at Toro in Chicago Nice dishware is worthwhile at home, too. “I’d love to receive items from Ivo Angel, a beautiful ceramics company out of Italy. I am a huge fan of the splatter design and always want a pinch bowl; I can’t have too many. Also the olive bowl with an attached vessel for pits is perfect for hosting.” —Julia Jaksoc, chef and owner of Bar Roza, Cafe Roze and Roze Pony in Nashville The pepper mill that chefs swear by. “It’s one of those tools that gets used constantly, makes a real difference, and is something every cook or bartender would appreciate having.” —Marco Torres, Chef at Brass and The Tusk Bar in New York City Fun socks. “Being locked down in heavy black pants, unforgiving non-slip shoe leathers, and a stiff chef coat means you have to find your personality somewhere. A pair of loud, ridiculous socks underneath always makes me feel a little more human. I’ll never forget getting this pair of bright yellow Spam socks as a Christmas gift one year. Honestly, it’s one of the best presents I’ve ever unwrapped, and it brings a little joy each time I slip them on.” —Soo Ahn, chef/partner at Adalina Prime, Arla and Adalina Italian in Chicago Something to take the edge off. “For the industry pro who enjoys a little puff puff and a good nap (especially after a Saturday morning shift with lines out the door), you can’t go wrong with Tokin’ Jew rolling papers. We sell them at the deli because, come on, but they’re also a fantastic gift. And for the pipe people, their pickle pipes are another way to keep it kosher.” —Jake Schneider, chef and co-owner of Schneider Deli in Chicago A beautiful book for recipe writing. “I would gift this brown leather journal cover from Shinola along with this 12-pack of pens. I think the notebook is a worthwhile splurge, and while I know the idea of a more expensive and elegant pen is both compelling and sexy, it is also impractical for when you’re on the go or as prone to losing nice pens as I am. These ones write fluidly and beautifully.” —Róbert LeBlanc, creative director and founder of LeBlanc + Smith in New Orleans The kitchen fit of your dreams. “I could wear this jumpsuit 24/7! It’s comfortable, easy to move around in, and perfect for those long days in the kitchen when I’m constantly running around and want something that looks as good as it feels.” —Andrea Belfiore, chef and founder of EVÈNTO in New York City A tool for foraging. “I love my ARS pruning shears. I take them pretty much everywhere when I’m out foraging, and they’re great for everything from cutting herbs to collecting branches and other ingredients for drinks. They’re one of those tools I use all the time.” —Danny Childs, co-owner of Field Day in Philadelphia A trio of pastry chef staples. “On any given day, a pastry professional will produce dozens of recipes, and we need tools to measure mass/weight, time, and temperature. Even when we have our own, backups or better ones are always welcome! My top picks include: this scale, which has a pull-out screen when you’re scaling on to sheet trays or large bowls; this kitchen timer has four color-coded channels for timing multiple projects at once; and this thermometer, which is fast-reading, accurate, and has a magnet on the back for easy access on any magnetic surface.” —Orlando Soto, executive pastry chef of Le Bernardin in New York City The perfect vessel for an industry-favorite amaro (or 50/50 shot). Some of the best hospitality happens in an ounce and a half: a pour of Cynar for a regular who had a long week, a welcome taste for someone new at the bar. I’d recommend these little ceramic artichoke shot glasses to make that moment feel even more considered.” —Steven Waters, owner and operator of Fino in Denver Many knife options. Patrick Dooley of Harry’s Bar in Paris recommends Le Grand Tradi, which is sized between a paring and chef’s knife, making it a great workhorse option, while Nancy Santiago, beverage director at NYC’s IGC Hospitality, recommends a Japanese petty knife “for precise citrus work and garnish prep.” Amir Babayoff of Ophelia Lounge in NYC is partial to Tojiro’s chef knives. And knife storage and upkeep options. Schneekloth of Toro recommends a knife backpack, while Devin Denzer, chef at Atsumeru in Chicago, recommends a whetstone and ceramic sharpening rod, especially for newer line cooks. A thoughtful gift card. “Here are a few gifts that I have received that stood out to me: a hefty gift card to a sought-after restaurant with guaranteed reservations on a night off, which is such a good way to give someone a night out; a gift card to a shoe store that carries high-quality work shoes, like Red Wings, Dansko, or Blundstones; and a gift card to something wellness-related—my business partner Jesse got me three sessions at a body-stretching spa downtown.” —Phila Lorn, chef and co-owner of Mawn and Sao in Philadelphia Responses have been edited and condensed for clarity.

item.title: The dance floor that’s seen it all: inside 7 of the most spectacular parties at the storied Claridge’s ballroom
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
“From the era of Jane Austen to the age of AI, Claridge's has been a constant presence in the heart of Mayfair,” historian Martin Williams explains. He takes another sip of tea, served in aquamarine and white china, as we sit in one of London's most storied ballrooms inside one of the world's most legendary hotels. Claridge’s, which first opened its doors in 1812, has drawn glittering guests like Queen Victoria ever since it opened. But during the Roaring Twenties, the Art Deco hotel became an English institution, attracting royalty and Hollywood stars through its checkered-floor expanse. Now, Williams has penned the hotel’s official biography, Claridge’s: Queen of Hotels, Hotel of Kings, looking back at some of the most lavish events, and showing just why – over 200 years on – Claridge's remains one of the best hotels in the world. On the day we meet, it's 9am on a brisk and sunny London morning and, funnily enough, we're the only ones wandering around Claridge's ballroom at this hour, but these walls have seen everyone from Queen Elizabeth II to the Queen Mother and Princess Diana, Cecil Beaton, Charlie Chaplin, Elsa Schiaparelli and Isabella Blow attending an extravagant celebration or two beneath its Art Deco chandeliers. “From debutante dances to fashion shows, this room has played host to innumerable glittering occasions,” Williams explains. "The celebrities who have found themselves within these walls are almost too many to mention.” But here's a proper go, looking through the storied ballroom's most memorable affairs… Queen Elizabeth II's royal wedding after-party that Nicky Haslam called “the best party I've ever been to” in July 1981 Hours after Prince Charles and Lady Diana's tied the knot at St Paul's Cathedral in July 1981, Queen Elizabeth II attended a party hosted in her honour by her cousin Lady Elizabeth Shakerley in Claridge’s ballroom. The lavish affair was packed to the nines with kings, queens and countless princes and princesses. “She was accompanied by virtually the entire British royal family,” Williams explains. “The private party was attended by everybody from Princess Grace of Monaco to US First Lady, Nancy Reagan. On that occasion, footage from the recent royal wedding was played on an endless loop as Lester Lanin played for hours on end and champagne flowed. Society decorator Nicky Haslam subsequently described it as the best party he'd ever been to.” A game of cricket in the ballroom in 1933 “I'm particularly intrigued by the cricket-themed lunch that took place here in 1933," William shares. "On that occasion, the floor was laid with turf. The staff and guests all wore whites and balling and batting took place on a fully sized pitch between the tables.” The fabled ‘Olympian Ball’ of March 1935 “One of the most glittering affairs that took place in this room was the Olympian Ball of 1935 when the cream of London society dressed up as gods and goddesses, nymphs and fawns and other figures from classical mythology to raise money for charity,” Williams says. “Lady Isabel Manners came as Diana, with two enormous dogs straining on leads; Lady Mary Lygon as Amphitrite arrived in a chariot shaped like a sea shell; Mrs Bryan Guinness was a pearl-studded Venus; and the couturiere Elsa Schiaparelli was a dramatic Stella.” The legendary outfits left a big mark on the gossip columns. “When the inhabitants of Mount Olympus come to town, wrote one bedazzled gossip columnist, they're bound to cause something of a stir”. Unlike the wild theatrics of the Olympian Ball, the Cygnet's Ball was all about the formal world of debutantes and etiquette, as it was the annual society dance bringing together young women from London's fashionable finishing schools and eligible members of London's upper class. The 1955 event was captured by celebrated society photographer Slim Aarons, who captured the exclusive formal event and its elegant attendees. Audrey Hepburn's Roman Holiday welcome home party in May 1953 “Then a relative unknown, Audrey Hepburn had a highly significant meeting with director William Wyler here at Claridge's. And on the back of that meeting, he awarded her the part of Princess Ann in Roman Holiday. After filming Roman Holiday in, of course, Rome, opposite Gregory Peck, Audrey Hepburn celebrated with a party here at Claridge's on the eve of her emergence as a major Hollywood star." She would then go on to win the Academy Award for Best Actress in March 1954, aged just 24. Queen Elizabeth and Princess Margaret private fashion show in November 1952 Shortly before she was coronated, a then-Princess Elizabeth was joined by her sister Princess Margaret to attend a private fashion parade held by the Incorporated Society of London Fashion Designers. The glittering young royals were there to look at the fabrics and styles from the biggest names in British couture, spanning 11 leading fashion houses, including British dressmaker Sir Norman Hartnell who designed Queen Elizabeth II’s June 1953 coronation dress. Diane von Furstenberg's Jazz Aged-themed supper in June 2010 In slightly more recent history, Belgian-American fashion designer Diane von Furstenberg hosted a star-studded Jazz Age-themed supper in Claridge’s ballroom in 2010 to celebrate the new rooms and suites she designed for the hotel. The lavish party was a who's who of the 2010s celebrity scene, with everyone from Victoria Beckham and a “trilby-topped” Madonna to Joan Collins and Tracey Emin in attendance. Von Furstenberg spoke of her love affair with Claridge's during her speech, saying “[Claridge's] is the only place they still say 'Highness' when I walk in those wonderful doors”. "It has been an amazing adventure," she went on. “If walls could talk, these rooms could write books and books and books”. 16 years on, she's in luck.

item.title: How We Brought a Taste of Maine to Bon Appétit LIVE
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Attendees of Bon Appétit Live experienced a taste of Maine through a hands-on lobster cooking class and a demonstration of wild blueberry cornmeal shortcakes, both hosted by Visit Maine. The class, Lobster 101, was led by Bon Appétit manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Attendees learned how to break down a whole, steamed two-pound Maine lobster and transform the meat into a rich, creamy lobster dip—ideal for holiday hosting. Guests then enjoyed the fruits of their labor, sampling the freshly made dip with Ritz crackers before tasting oysters. Tripp explained that her oysters, cultivated in the cold tidal waters of the Lower Weskeag River, take three years to reach maturity. Known for their distinctive fluted shells, they offer a briny, mineral-rich flavor balanced by a mellow sweetness. After years as a lobster harvester, Tripp started Aphrodite Oysters to diversify her lobster business and has since shifted her focus to oyster cultivation full-time. She’s come to appreciate the many environmental benefits of farming and consuming them. Her oysters filter up to 50 gallons of water a day, taking in nitrogen and sequestering some for their growing shells. “Eating an oyster is contributing to the environment,” she declared. Indeed, water test scores have improved at her farm, demonstrating that bivalves help create a healthier ecosystem. Before the end of the class, a few brave attendees volunteered to shuck their first oysters. Krista guided them through the process, demonstrating how to safely do it at home by protecting the hand holding the shellfish with a towel and gently working the knife into the hinge until the shell released. The well-earned reward was another taste of the Penobscot Bay, as fresh and pristine as the waters themselves. Later in the day, guests in the Demo Kitchen were treated to Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote, prepared by Bon Appétit senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk. The compote featured wild Maine blueberries from Brodis Blueberries, a multigenerational family farm in Hope, Maine, stewarded by Ron Howard and his family. Howard joined Szewczyk for the demo, where he shared that 99% of the wild blueberries grown and harvested in the United States come from Maine. Attendees learned that they have been growing since the end of the Ice Age, when the tenacious plants, fortified by ericoid mycorrhizal fungi, began to grow and colonize the newly exposed land as glaciers retreated. An important food source for Native Americans, wild blueberries were valued by Indigenous communities for their nutritional benefits well before the modern superfood movement. Speaking passionately, Howard discussed the many challenges facing Maine growers, including tariffs and currency exchange fluctuations, particularly the impact of a stronger Canadian dollar. Like many Maine farmers, the family has had to get creative. Howard invested in new equipment, including a more efficient type of harvester that allowed the business to scale up and sell to retailers. They created a shelf-stable, freeze-dried product with no added ingredients, allowing them to ship their product beyond the local area. Howard and his son started a distillery, where they use wild blueberries to make an eau de vie and vodka. They have also begun hosting a Wild Blueberry Weekend, opening the doors to the farm and educating the public about the unique benefits of their crop and their growing process. Carolann Ouellette, director of the Maine Office of Tourism, emphasized that visiting Maine and engaging with local growers and producers such as Howard and Tripp was the best way to experience the state’s diverse bounty. “The relationship between people and nature is inseparable, and stewardship is an important part of the state's identity,” she reflected. Ouellette grew up in New Jersey but relocated to Maine over 40 years ago. Her family used to visit Maine when she was a child, and she recalls those experiences vividly: “As a kid, I remember, when you get to Maine, you can smell the pie or smell the spruce.” It’s those potent memories that drew her to the state permanently, a place she described as “filled with hardworking, welcoming communities that depend on one another.” A few years ago, Visit Maine began placing greater emphasis on the state’s culinary identity. Ouellette said that awareness of Maine as a food destination continues to grow, “Sea to table with local ingredients is what we were doing before it was a thing.” Beyond the lobster, Visit Maine has been intentional about showcasing the breadth of the state’s agricultural, fishing, and heritage industries. Apples, potatoes, kelp, seaweed, and grains are just a few of the local ingredients featured in Visit Maine’s newsletter and Bountiful Plate video series, which highlights food and beverage producers throughout the state. Ouellette noted that Maine’s food culture is more diverse than many people expect, and its abundance of local products has attracted an interesting mix of exceptional chefs, many of whom are deeply embedded in their communities. Ouellette cited Tripp’s practice of personally delivering her oysters to local restaurants as an example of how the hospitality ecosystem is interconnected. Most important, Ouellette emphasized that sustainability and stewardship are central to the state’s approach to its food systems and relationship with the landscape. “You can’t get much fresher than food in Maine,” she concluded. Bon Appétit LIVE 2026 was sponsored by East Fork, Visit Maine, and S.Pellegrino® Sparkling Natural Mineral Water with thanks to All-Clad, As Ever, Bachan’s, Better Sour, Field Company, Floura, Gimme Seaweed, GOODLES, Graza, Hedley & Bennett, Kann Coffee, Material Kitchen, Misen, Owala®, Rip Van, SharkNinja, and Staub.

item.title: IDEA: Under-the-Radar Overlanding Spots in the West, According to a Full-Timer
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Jay Clue has clocked more than 50,000 miles exploring the rugged beauty of North America while chasing stars, stories, and dark skies in his custom-built Jeep Rubicon overland rig. (Photo: Jay Clue) There is a specific moment, usually about ten or twenty miles after the asphalt dissolves into dirt, when the noise of the modern world begins to cut out completely. The cell bars drop to zero, the tourist traffic vanishes in your rearview mirror, and the real adventure begins. But planning a camping trip these days feels almost like buying concert tickets. You wait months for a release date, log onto a park website, fight for a reservation, and ultimately end up with your tent pitched a few feet from an RV, falling asleep to the soul-soothing sound of their generator howling through the night. Even as a full-time overlander, I’d love to say I gave up on the asphalt lottery long ago, but sadly, for some places, it’s the only way left to experience them. True wilderness is still out there, though. Finding it just means trading the pavement for dirt tracks and exploration. While social media loves to showcase six-figure custom trucks wrapped in tactical gear, crawling through hood-deep mud or hanging off thousand-foot cliffs, the real secret to overlanding isn’t in the extremes. It’s about finding your own beautiful piece of serenity in the backcountry. At its heart, overlanding is simply vehicle-based travel. In other words, using your rig as a mobile backpack to carry your kitchen, bed, and gear deeper into the wild than any paved road could ever take you. You don’t need a custom-built rock crawler or axle-breaking trails. All you need is a dirt track, a map, and your sense of adventure. When you want to trade packed-out front-country campgrounds for untouched wilderness, finding that solitude usually just means looking where others aren’t—whether that’s adventuring down unnamed forest trails or taking that random side road just to see where it goes. I can’t give away all my secret spots. But here are three of my favorite under-the-radar areas to get you started on your overlanding exploration list. A few hours southeast of Salt Lake City’s hustle and bustle lies a massive geologic upheaval, sculpted over millions of years by wind and water into one of Utah’s best-kept secrets. Spanning roughly 2,000 square miles—an expanse nearly the size of Delaware—the Swell makes “massive” feel like an understatement. The San Rafael Swell is a true overlander’s playground, crisscrossed by hundreds of miles of dirt tracks winding past towering red-rock formations, sweeping desert vistas, hidden canyons, and jagged sandstone ribs. Unlike Utah’s famed Mighty 5 national parks, reaching the heart of the Swell demands some serious off-pavement miles, naturally filtering out the crowds and leaving its wildest treasures to those willing to earn them. Beyond the driving, the Swell is an open-air museum packed with history. You can spend days searching for dinosaur tracks, hundreds of Native American rock art panels, weathered pioneer homesteads, and abandoned Cold War uranium mines. When night falls, the region has some of the darkest skies in the Beehive State, making it one of my favorite places to stay up until dawn photographing the Milky Way. And once the sun crests the horizon, the adventure shifts into high gear—whether you’re squeezing through narrow slot canyons, tackling desert climbs, hiking rim overlooks, or cooling off from the high-desert heat with a lazy river float. Every time I head into the Swell, the web of backcountry trails feels virtually endless. The 27–mile Behind the Reef OHV route stands out as a personal favorite, though you can easily link dirt corridors to push even farther—connecting straight into Capitol Reef’s iconic Cathedral Valley or the surreal, lunar badlands of Mancos Shale. Best of all, with the vast majority of this rugged landscape open to free dispersed camping, you don’t just pass through the San Rafael Swell—you get to wake up right in the middle of it. While mainstream travelers crowd the beautiful Pacific coast, southeastern Oregon remains one of the quietest stretches of public land in the country. Spanning nearly 30,000 square miles and home to the world’s largest International Dark Sky Sanctuary, the Oregon Outback isn’t a single destination—it is a sweeping, multi-day dirt journey through a forgotten corner of the American West. Rolling east along lonely gravel ribbons, the landscape unfolds in dramatic waves. On the western edge, sheer 3,000-foot basalt cliffs rise abruptly above sun-bleached alkali lake beds at the Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge. Camping on the high plateau puts you steps away from Hart Mountain Hot Springs, where you can soak in a stone-lined thermal pool under an endless canopy of stars while pronghorn antelope graze quietly in the surrounding sagebrush. Farther east, the desert floor gives way to the towering fault-block wall of Steens Mountain. The unpaved Steens Mountain Loop Road climbs past 9,000 feet through shimmering aspen groves, opening up to breathtaking, glacier-carved valleys like Kiger Gorge that feel lifted straight out of the Swiss Alps. To cap off the traverse, drop down to the Alvord Desert playa, more than a mile below Steens’ summit, then head toward the Idaho border, where the horizon fractures into the Owyhee Canyonlands. Winding dirt tracks drop you between towering, honeycombed volcanic spires and deep river canyons that glow fiery orange at sunset. With cell service, fuel, and pavement fading far into your rearview mirror, this vast corridor rewards prepared travelers with the rarest luxury on the road: total, uninterrupted silence. If I hadn’t driven this route earlier this summer, I probably wouldn’t have included it here. Because it sits just east of the famed North Cascades National Park, I assumed the area would be choked with tourists and far from an under-the-radar overlanding destination. One cloudy afternoon, on a whim, I decided to explore it anyway. To my surprise, I passed only two vehicles on the entire climb and spotted just one more at the summit. This area delivers some of the most dramatic views in the entire Cascade Range, yet I had the ridge completely to myself at sunset—watching the day sink behind endless jagged, snowcapped peaks before the sky ignited in fluorescent pinks and oranges. The highest drivable road in Washington, this single-lane dirt route clings to a thousand-foot-high cliff wall along Deadhorse Point with zero guardrails. That immense drop-off not only demands steady nerves around the blind corners, but also acts as a natural filter, keeping standard RVs and casual weekenders away. Once you clear the shelf, quiet, primitive campsites sit tucked near the timberline at over 6,100 feet. From camp, you can step right onto the Pacific Crest Trail, or push your rig farther onto two distinct offshoots. The rocky Slate Peak spur climbs steeply toward the 7,400-foot summit area for views stretching to Mount Baker. For a tougher, high-clearance run, Chancellor Road drops down the western slope through rugged, rocky terrain toward the 1890s mining ruins of Barron and the trailhead for the Chancellor ghost town. At the end of the day, the best campsites don’t come with reservation numbers, and they rarely show up on a top-ten list. Use these routes as a launch pad, then keep going—pick a dusty turnoff you’ve never heard of, respect the land you cross, and discover the magic that happens when you leave the crowds behind. Jay Clue is a professional photographer and Outside contributor who made the switch to overlanding full-time in 2024. Since then, he has clocked more than 50,000 miles exploring the rugged beauty of North America while chasing stars, stories, and dark skies in his custom-built Jeep Rubicon overland rig. After hundreds of nights photographing the backcountry, he can happily report there’s only been one rare occasion when he thought that he was about to be abducted by aliens.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Boost the Performance of Your Canister Stove Without Blowing it Up
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy I had just finished pitching my tent and inflating my sleeping pad on a recent trip, and I could not wait to tear open the packet of dried miso soup I’d packed. My fingers were chilled from fiddling with guylines, and I craved the feeling of a steaming cup cradled in my hands. I screwed my ultralight stove onto a fuel canister, squeezed some water from my filter bag into a pot, and lit up. And then I proceeded to wait for what felt like ages. The flame was low and weak. Had I packed a nearly empty canister? No. The feeble flame was a harbinger, much like the leaves littering the trail: Winter was coming. Canister stoves, like the ones most backpackers use during the summer hiking season, perform poorly when the mercury drops. Cold temperatures lower the internal pressure of the canister, causing it to falter, sputter, or produce a smaller flame. Regular winter campers often solve this problem by packing liquid fuel stoves like the MSR Whisperlite, which perform well in below freezing temperatures. Some canister stoves have a built-in pressure regulator that helps them stay efficient in the cold. But not every backpacker wants to shell out for an entire quiver of camp stoves. That’s where a little innovation comes in: Keeping a canister warm, even when the ambient temperature is frigid, helps maintain pressure so you can boil water on a regular canister stove all year round. Do it the wrong way, however and you might end up scorching more than your food. When it comes to boosting the efficiency of your canister stove in winter, the key is gentle warming. A fuel canister’s contents are pressurized; when it is cold out, your goal is to increase that pressure ever so slightly. But overheating—and thus overpressurizing—can cause the canister to explode. Warnings printed on the side of a canister tell this tale. Most manufacturers caution users to keep a canister below 120°F. Heating a canister by rapid means, like placing it in boiling water is a very bad idea—just ask the guy who punched a hole in his ceiling trying to heat a canister for a fuel transfer. How else can one warm a canister? One hiker on Reddit suggested sticking a chemical hand warmer next to the canister and enclosing it in an insulated pouch. But experts Backpacker spoke to did not recommend that method. “You’re adding a continuous heat source while also insulating the canister, and there’s no particularly good way to monitor or control its temperature,” says Adam Wilcox, senior mechanical design engineer at Jetboil. Hothands, manufacturer of popular chemical warmers, claims that their products reach an average of 135°F, and warns that the maximum temperature can surpass 158°F. Granted, this doesn’t mean that placing a hand warmer beside your fuel canister will immediately warm the fuel contents to that same temperature, but it does heighten your risk of dangerously increasing the pressure. Gentle warming is a safer bet. “Body heat before use or a controlled warm-water bath are much more predictable ways of warming a cold canister,” says Wilcox. “The key with water is warm, not hot, and avoiding excessive heating of the canister.” For a quick boil, keeping the fuel canister inside your jacket for a few minutes prior to use may do the trick to increase internal pressure. Of course, the effects of this will diminish rather quickly as you run your stove and expose the canister to cold air. If you need to run your stove a little longer to cook a meal or melt snow, a warm water bath can provide safe, continuous warming. Place your fuel canister inside a dish or spare pot. (I like to carry a collapsible silicone bowl for this purpose.) Light your stove. As soon as the water begins to warm but before it boils, pour some into the dish surrounding your canister. You should immediately notice improved performance. Shopping for a new stove? Springing for one with a pressure regulator can help it perform more consistently across seasons. MSR claims that its Pocket Rocket Deluxe can run at full power at a fuel canister pressure of as little as 16.5 PSI. (A full canister would typically be at 45 PSI at room temperature.)
